star.紫微.label: Zi Wei
star.紫微.summary: Zi Wei belongs to Earth. The *Complete Book* calls it the most honoured star of the central heavens, the imperial seat, ruling over career. In Zi Wei Dou Shu its role is less about being the most fortunate star than about setting position: where all fourteen major stars fall is worked out from Zi Wei, so it is the chart's point of reference. In temperament it is usually described as taking on responsibility, keeping a sense of proportion and not wanting to lose face. Note that the *Complete Book* also says Zi Wei without its two aides, Zuo Fu and You Bi, is a lonely ruler: with or without that support, it reads completely differently. So reading Zi Wei is never just about which palace it sits in, but about who is beside it. Whether it is strong, and whether it has support, are the two questions to ask first.
star.紫微.full:
Zi Wei belongs to Earth. The *Complete Book* opens by describing it as the most honoured star of the central heavens, the imperial seat that holds the pivot of creation; the table of star attributes in Book Two records it as a star of the central heavens, transforming into the imperial seat and ruling over career. Read together, these describe a structural position: Zi Wei is not the most fortunate of the fourteen stars, but the one that decides where the other thirteen go.

Its meanings cover a cluster of words: leading, carrying responsibility, standards, dignity. Zi Wei tends to take things on itself, and to measure by its own yardstick. This is a stance, not a fixed outcome. The *Complete Book* is clear that without its aides it is a lonely ruler, and that its power to bring blessings and dispel misfortune depends on whether it is strong and on what favourable or difficult stars accompany it. The same Zi Wei reads one way with support and another without; one way strong and another weak.

So in this book Zi Wei never forms a conclusion on its own. It is always read together with Zuo Fu and You Bi, Tian Xiang, Wen Chang and Wen Qu, and always with the question of what conditions its four directions give it. The old writers were in fact quite reserved about an isolated imperial star.

It should be said plainly: Zi Wei in the Life Palace does not mean high status, nor a forceful personality. It describes a tendency and a sense of position, not a person's achievements or worth.

There is one more common mistake to avoid when reading Zi Wei: taking it to mean good fortune. In Book Two of the *Complete Book*, the verdicts for Zi Wei in each palace range from favourable to unfavourable, and the difference lies entirely in which stars share or face its palace. This book therefore reads Zi Wei only as a sense of position and a tendency to carry responsibility, and says what stands beside it every time it is mentioned. Without that, the name Zi Wei would be nothing more than an empty title to the reader.

star.天機.label: Tian Ji
star.天機.summary: Tian Ji belongs to Wood and is the third star of the Southern Dipper. The *Complete Book* says it transforms into goodness, and Book Two records it as ruling over siblings. Its key words are movement and thought: adaptable, quick to react, thinking a great deal. Master Yuchan says it assists the emperor's commands and eases the course of misfortune, so its position is one of support and turning things around, not command. For the same reason, Tian Ji's strength depends heavily on its surroundings: strong where it is bright, powerless where it is weak, as the *Complete Book* puts it directly. Reading Tian Ji means looking at what around it gives it room to act. Its combinations with Tian Liang, Tai Yin and Ju Men each have their own names in the old texts, and read quite differently.
star.天機.full:
Tian Ji belongs to Wood. The *Complete Book* calls it the third star of the Southern Dipper, a good star that extends one's reckoning, transforming into goodness; the attribute table in Book Two records it as transforming into goodness in the Southern Dipper and ruling over siblings. Together these two labels, goodness and siblings, describe a position of dealing with people and smoothing things over on their behalf.

Its meanings cover a cluster of words: adaptability, deliberation, learning, turning points. Tian Ji's strength is thinking fast and turning fast; its weakness lies in the same place, thinking too much and moving too often. In Master Yuchan's words, it assists the emperor's commands and eases the course of misfortune: it is good at turning things around and adjusting, not at holding out by force.

The *Complete Book* is especially direct about the conditions for Tian Ji's strength: strong where it is bright, powerless where it is weak. This is worth remembering, because it reminds us that Tian Ji is not a self-sufficient star. Well placed, with favourable stars to draw on, its adaptability works; when conditions are lacking, the same quickness shows up as wavering and difficulty settling.

When this book reads Tian Ji, the focus is on whether it has room to act, not on whether it is clever. The first can be seen on the chart; the second cannot.

The old texts give special names to Tian Ji's combinations with other major stars: Ji Yue Tong Liang, Tian Ji with Ju Men, Tian Ji with Tian Liang. These read quite differently, and the schools don't always agree. In this book's rules, such patterns are held back for review: when they are triggered is a matter of geometry and can be checked, but what they mean needs textual support. Until the sources are complete, these names will not appear in the body of a book.

One last point: Tian Ji's adaptability is often read as intelligence, but intelligence can't be seen on a chart. What it describes is a way of handling things: a tendency to go around rather than through, to think one step further rather than act first. In situations that call for flexibility, that is a strength; in situations that call for persistence, it becomes wavering.

star.太陽.label: Tai Yang
star.太陽.summary: Tai Yang belongs to Fire. The *Complete Book* calls it the essence of the sun and the outward model of creation; Book Two records it as ruling over career and transforming into nobility. Its meanings revolve around shining: outward-facing, giving, being seen. Tai Yang cares most about position. Master Yuchan lists it palace by palace: rising in the Yin and Mao positions, the sun at midday in the Wu position, setting in the You position, and losing its light in the Xu, Hai and Zi positions. Of the fourteen stars, the same Tai Yang varies in strength across palaces more visibly than almost any other. So to talk about Tai Yang without saying which palace it falls in is to say very little. In a man's chart the old texts treat Tai Yang as the father star, and in a woman's also as the husband star; that is the old framework, and this book takes only the part that concerns the reader.
star.太陽.full:
Tai Yang belongs to Fire. The *Complete Book* calls it the essence of the sun, and says it is the outward model of creation, giving a person a noble air; the attribute table in Book Two records it as transforming into nobility in both Dippers and ruling over career. Nobility here means position and visibility, not wealth and not social rank.

Its meanings cover a cluster of words: lighting up, giving, showing outwardly, responsibility. Tai Yang's energy points outwards: it tends to look after others, represent the group, and bring matters into the open. In return, it is easily worn down in positions where it isn't seen.

Of the fourteen major stars, Tai Yang is among the most sensitive to position. Master Yuchan lists it place by place: rising in the Yin and Mao positions, ascending the hall in Chen and Si, the sun at midday in Wu; setting in You, noble but not prominent, refined but without substance; and losing its light in Xu, Hai and Zi. This is not a score of good and bad, but a difference in strength and in how it shows. A Tai Yang that has lost its light is not bad; its shining turns inwards and works more slowly.

This book always reads Tai Yang together with its palace and its strength, and together with Tai Yin: the *Complete Book* says what the sun and moon most dislike is facing away from each other. They are a pair, not two separate stars.

The *Complete Book* treats Tai Yang as the father star, and says that with light it is favourable and without light it harms the father. This book does not use such verdicts: its principles explicitly forbid inferring what happens to a reader's parents from the reader's own chart. Here Tai Yang is used only to understand the reader: whom you tend to look after, where you are seen, and where you tend to spin your wheels. How family members fare belongs to their own charts, not this one.

One more point: Tai Yang governs nobility, but nobility is not status, nor income. When the *Complete Book* uses the word, it means being seen, being entrusted with things, standing in the open. A person can be rich without that kind of nobility, and can have a great deal of it within a very small circle. When this book talks about Tai Yang, it uses phrases like visibility and the position you carry, avoiding any suggestion of rank.

star.武曲.label: Wu Qu
star.武曲.summary: Wu Qu belongs to Metal and is the sixth star of the Northern Dipper. The *Complete Book* names it twice as the ruler of the Wealth Palace. Its meaning is more about execution than accumulation: firm, decisive, intent on getting things done. The *Complete Book* says it governs lifespan in heaven and wealth in the chart, and that it is firm and decisive, given to joy and anger, capable of bringing blessings or trouble; both sides come from the same quality. Note that Wu Qu does not mean being wealthy: it describes a way of handling resources, and how much there is is another matter. Read it together with the whole structure of the Wealth Palace. When it shares a palace with Tan Lang, Po Jun or Qi Sha, the old verdicts differ greatly, and it has to be read with the whole structure.
star.武曲.full:
Wu Qu belongs to Metal. Book One of the *Complete Book* calls it the sixth star of the Northern Dipper, ruler of the Wealth Palace; the attribute table in Book Two records it as transforming into wealth in the Northern Dipper and ruling over wealth. The two agree, making it the most clearly labelled of the fourteen major stars.

Its meanings cover a cluster of words: decisiveness, execution, practicality, bearing costs. What marks Wu Qu is turning ideas into action: no detours, and little patience for waiting. The *Complete Book* describes it as firm and decisive, given to joy and anger, capable of bringing blessings or trouble. Strengths and costs are written into the same sentence, and that is worth keeping as it is. Firmness gets things done, and can also hurt people, oneself included.

The *Complete Book* also records an often-quoted line: Wu Qu in the Life Palace brings no small blessing, but its partner Tan Lang does not flourish in youth. It describes a rhythm: Wu Qu's strength often doesn't show early. That is a tendency, not a timetable, and this book never turns it into something that will happen at a particular age.

Finally: ruling over wealth is not the same as having wealth. Wu Qu describes how you treat resources: how you earn, how you spend, how you judge what's worth it. How much you have can't be seen on a chart, and shouldn't be inferred from one.

When Wu Qu shares a palace with Tan Lang, Po Jun or Qi Sha, the old verdicts vary enormously, from rising to high command to isolation and loss. Most of these differences come from different editions rather than different conclusions of one logic. This book keeps only what the schools agree on, that Wu Qu governs execution and decisiveness, and marks the disagreements rather than reconciling them on its own.

Also, the label ruler of wealth does not support any investment or financial advice. This book's principles forbid treating a rating as a basis for buying or selling.

star.天同.label: Tian Tong
star.天同.summary: Tian Tong belongs to Water and is the fourth star of the Southern Dipper. The *Complete Book* records it as master of the Wellbeing Palace, transforming into blessing. Its meanings revolve around ease: gentle, accommodating, knowing how to enjoy life, and prone to settling for things as they are. The *Complete Book* describes Tian Tong people as honest and clean-handed, with unusual looks, and says its blessing most welcomes favourable stars that add to it. The blessing here isn't good luck but a state of being content in oneself. And precisely because it is content, Tian Tong's usual challenge isn't hardship but drive: it needs a push from outside to leave a comfortable place. The old texts actually rate it higher alongside malefic stars, because Tian Tong needs some resistance; this is often misread as hardship being good for you.
star.天同.full:
Tian Tong belongs to Water. Book One of the *Complete Book* calls it the fourth star of the south, master of the Wellbeing Palace; the attribute table in Book Two records it as transforming into blessing in the Southern Dipper and ruling over wellbeing, with its elements noted as Water and Metal. The label points to an inner state rather than outward achievement.

Its meanings cover a cluster of words: mildness, accommodation, contentment, enjoyment. Tian Tong's strength is not competing with people and making life comfortable; its cost is the same thing, because comfort itself weakens the reasons to move. That isn't a flaw, it's a structure. The *Complete Book* says its blessing most welcomes favourable stars that add to it; put the other way, without stimulation Tian Tong's showing is rather flat.

So Tian Tong depends especially on the conditions brought by the stars in its palace and its four directions. With malefic stars alongside, the old texts often rate it higher, not because malefics are good, but because Tian Tong needs a little resistance. This book writes that only as a tendency and a condition, never as a claim that you must suffer to amount to something.

It should be said: ruling over wellbeing does not mean life goes smoothly, nor that there is no pressure. It describes how you settle yourself, not what happens to you.

One common misreading deserves a special warning: taking Tian Tong needs resistance to mean hardship is good for you. The old texts say the structure of the palace changes how it shows, not that difficulty has value in itself. When writing about Tian Tong, this book avoids anything that justifies hardship; its principles are explicit on this, ruling out both motivational consolation and fatalistic rationalising.

star.廉貞.label: Lian Zhen
star.廉貞.summary: Lian Zhen belongs to Fire and is the fifth star of the Northern Dipper. The *Complete Book* says that in the Dipper it governs rank, and in the chart it governs authority and command. It carries the most complicated labels of the fourteen major stars: Book Two records it at once as transforming into the imprisoned and the forceful, as ruler of career in the Career Palace, and as a secondary romance star in the Life and Body Palaces. All three point to the same quality: intensity. Lian Zhen's energy is about commitment, whether to principles, work or feelings. The *Complete Book* says that when it is not strong and meets official trouble, the imprisoned turns forceful; the emphasis is on conditions, not on a fixed outcome. It reads one way in the Life and Body Palaces and another in the Career Palace, and mixing the two produces a completely different person. Its element is Fire and its nature urgent, with clear differences in strength depending on its placement.
star.廉貞.full:
Lian Zhen belongs to Fire. Book One of the *Complete Book* calls it the fifth star of the Northern Dipper, which in the Dipper governs rank and in the chart governs authority and command; the attribute table in Book Two gives it three labels at once: transforming into the imprisoned and the forceful in the Northern Dipper, ruler of career in the Career Palace, and secondary romance star in the Life and Body Palaces. That one star has so many faces is itself its defining feature.

Its meanings cover commitment, principle, rules, and also the intensity of feeling. Lian Zhen is not good at lukewarm: it puts a great deal of itself into what it cares about, and is quite cold towards what it doesn't. That gap looks very different in different palaces: in the Career Palace it shows as exacting standards and rule-keeping, in the Life and Body Palaces as emotion and attraction.

The phrase the imprisoned turns forceful is the most often misread line about Lian Zhen. The original says that when it is not strong and also meets official trouble, the imprisoned turns forceful: it describes how the star behaves when conditions are lacking, and the premise is written out plainly. This book reads it as what Lian Zhen looks like when constrained, never as a prediction of lawsuits or calamity; its principles also explicitly forbid inferring crime or legal outcomes from stars.

The point in reading Lian Zhen is where it puts its commitment, and whether its strength and the stars in its palace give it something worth committing to.

Book Two of the *Complete Book* lists Lian Zhen in the Life and Body Palaces separately from Lian Zhen in the Career Palace, and the distinction can't be dropped. In the Career Palace it reads as standards and exactness; in the Life and Body Palaces, as emotional intensity and attraction. Mix the two, and you read a person who doesn't exist.

This book also never uses Lian Zhen to infer romantic events or legal trouble. Secondary romance star is a label of meaning, not a prediction of behaviour; the book's principles put a hard stop on both kinds of inference.

star.天府.label: Tian Fu
star.天府.summary: Tian Fu belongs to Earth. The *Complete Book* calls it the first commanding star of the Southern Dipper, and Book Two records it as transforming into the star of command and ruling over wealth and property. It is the chart's other pivot alongside Zi Wei: the fourteen major stars divide into a Zi Wei group and a Tian Fu group, which mirror each other across the Yin–Shen line. In meaning, Tian Fu leans towards preserving, gathering in and stability; its strength is being able to hold things, not starting them. The *Complete Book* says that in the Dipper it is the lodge of blessing and authority, and with favourable stars it is the foundation of wealth and honour. The word is foundation: the base, not the result. The pattern it forms with Zi Wei is called the meeting of ruler and minister in the old texts, but whether that holds depends on whether the supporting stars are in place.
star.天府.full:
Tian Fu belongs to Earth. Book One of the *Complete Book* calls it the first commanding star of the Southern Dipper, master of wealth, the lodge of blessing and authority; the attribute table in Book Two records it as transforming into the star of command in the Southern Dipper and ruling over wealth and property. Wealth and property side by side point to holding and settling, not flow and acquisition.

Structurally, Tian Fu stands level with Zi Wei. The fourteen major stars are worked out as two groups, the Zi Wei group and the Tian Fu group, symmetrical across the Yin–Shen line; this is also why the number of empty palaces in a chart can only be zero, two or four. So Tian Fu is not just a star but a pivot.

Its meanings cover a cluster of words: preserving, gathering in, thoroughness, not rushing ahead. Tian Fu tends to make the base secure first and talk about everything else afterwards; its tolerance for risk is lower than Wu Qu's, and its tolerance for change lower than Qi Sha's or Po Jun's. The *Complete Book* says the foundation of wealth and honour, not wealth and honour, and the measure is exactly right: it gives base conditions, not results.

When reading Tian Fu, this book pays special attention to one thing: stability and conservatism are two names for the same quality, judged completely differently in different situations. So whether Tian Fu is good or bad can never be separated from what it is holding.

When Zi Wei and Tian Fu flank or face each other, the old texts call it the meeting of ruler and minister; the *Complete Book* has a line saying that when ruler and minister meet, the talent is fit to govern. But whether the pattern holds depends on whether the supporting stars are in place: without Zuo Fu and You Bi, Wen Chang and Wen Qu, or Tian Kui and Tian Yue, the meeting is only a name. This book holds such patterns back for review in its rules: the structure can be checked, but the meaning needs textual support before it is used.

star.太陰.label: Tai Yin
star.太陰.summary: Tai Yin is the essence of water. The *Complete Book* records it as ruler of property, transforming into wealth, and says it is the sun's partner. Tai Yang shines outwards; Tai Yin draws inwards, and its meanings revolve around accumulation, care, fine detail and private life. Tai Yin also cares greatly about position: the *Complete Book* treats the Mao, Chen, Si, Wu and Wei positions as its weak ground and the You, Xu, Hai, Zi and Chou positions as its own, and regards it as the mother star and one of the main stars of a woman's chart. Note that transforming into wealth describes the ability to gather and store, not an amount; a chart can't show how much money anyone has. Its position relative to Tai Yang often says more than which palace it sits in. Transforming into wealth is about how you gather and keep, not about sums, and this book says so repeatedly.
star.太陰.full:
Tai Yin is the essence of water. Book One of the *Complete Book* says it rules over property, transforms into wealth and is the sun's partner; the attribute table in Book Two records it as transforming into wealth in both Dippers and ruling over wealth and property. It and Tai Yang are a contrasting pair: Tai Yang shines, Tai Yin takes in.

Its meanings cover a cluster of words: accumulation, care, reserve, sensitivity to detail. Tai Yin's strength doesn't show in public occasions but in keeping things going: keeping a relationship going, keeping a home going, saving resources bit by bit. In return, it more easily draws its feelings inwards.

Tai Yin is as sensitive to position as Tai Yang. Master Xiyi records the Mao, Chen, Si, Wu and Wei positions as its weak ground, and the You, Xu, Hai, Zi and Chou positions as its own: daytime positions don't favour the moon, and night-time positions are where it belongs. This is a difference in strength, not in good and bad: a weak Tai Yin simply draws in more tightly and shows more slowly.

The *Complete Book* also treats Tai Yin as the mother star. This book handles that carefully: its principles explicitly forbid inferring a parent's health or circumstances from the reader's chart, so the label is used only to understand the reader's own way of caring, never turned round to comment on family.

Finally: transforming into wealth means a way of gathering and keeping, not an amount.

The *Complete Book* treats Tai Yin as both the mother star and one of the main stars of a woman's chart. That gender framework belongs to the old writers, and this book doesn't carry it over: a star's meaning shouldn't change according to the reader's gender. What we keep is what can be checked: Tai Yin takes in, accumulates and is sensitive to position. What we leave behind is the assignment of roles that grew out of it.

Transforming into wealth does not support any financial judgement either; the book's principles explicitly forbid it.

star.貪狼.label: Tan Lang
star.貪狼.summary: Tan Lang is the first star of the Northern Dipper. The *Complete Book* calls it the spirit that releases from hardship, transforming into romance and governing fortune and misfortune. Its meaning is desire: wanting, curiosity, wide interests, learning fast. The *Complete Book* says it can be swayed to good or ill, deceptive and scheming, or taught the arts of the immortals; both sides are set down together, because Tan Lang's direction is decided by what it wants, not by the star itself. That is why the old texts pay special attention to the stars sharing its palace: Huo Xing and Ling Xing, Lian Zhen, Di Kong and Di Jie each take the same desire somewhere very different. Alongside Huo Xing or Ling Xing it forms what the old texts call Fire Wolf or Bell Wolf; old and modern readings of these combinations differ considerably, and this book marks the disagreement.
star.貪狼.full:
Tan Lang belongs to Water and Wood. Book One of the *Complete Book* calls it the spirit of the Northern Dipper that releases from hardship, the first star, transforming into romance, the spirit that governs fortune and misfortune; the attribute table in Book Two records it as transforming into romance and force in the Northern Dipper, governing fortune and misfortune. Those last words matter: they say outright that Tan Lang itself does not decide good or bad.

Its meanings cover a cluster of words: desire, curiosity, talents, sociability, wide interests. Romance here means attraction in the broad sense, drawing and being drawn, not only love. Tan Lang's strengths are learning fast, wide interests and connecting easily with people; its challenge is focus, because when it wants too many things its strength scatters.

The *Complete Book* describes Tan Lang as deliberately two-sided: it can be swayed to good or ill, deceptive and scheming, or taught the arts of the immortals. The same star can run wild or follow a spiritual path, depending on what leads it. So Tan Lang depends more than any other major star on the conditions in its palace: with Huo Xing, with Ling Xing, with Lian Zhen, or meeting Di Kong and Di Jie, the old readings differ widely.

When handling Tan Lang, this book avoids two things: reading romance directly as romantic events, and reading desire as a moral judgement. Desire is a source of drive; where it points is the real question.

Huo Xing or Ling Xing in the same palace as Tan Lang forms what the old texts call Fire Wolf and Bell Wolf. Every school treats these as important combinations, but they disagree about what they mean. This book holds both patterns back for review in its rules: the trigger, sharing a palace, can be checked, but what they mean needs textual support, and at present there is only a single source. Until that is filled in, neither name will appear in the body of a book.

There is one more line to hold: the word for greed in Tan Lang's name is neutral in classical Chinese, meaning wanting, not a term of reproach. Reading it as a moral flaw contradicts the original and breaks the book's rule against judging character. This book describes the strength and direction of desire, not the worth of the person.

star.巨門.label: Ju Men
star.巨門.summary: Ju Men belongs to Water and Metal and is the second star of the Northern Dipper. The *Complete Book* calls it the star of yin essence, transforming into darkness, governing right and wrong. Darkness here isn't evil but the not-yet-clear: its meanings revolve around inquiry, questioning, and making clear what can't be seen. The *Complete Book* says flatly that in the Life or Body Palace it draws disputes and gossip all one's life; that is the old writers' view, and this book reads it as friction that comes from a way of speaking, not as trouble between people. Master Xiyi says that in the chart Ju Men handles right and wrong and governs what is obscure; the word handles is worth noticing, because handling disputes is not the same as creating them. Whether Tai Yang is placed to shine on it often matters more than Ju Men's own strength.
star.巨門.full:
Ju Men belongs to Water and Metal. Book One of the *Complete Book* calls it the second star of the Northern Dipper, the star of yin essence, transforming into darkness; the attribute table in Book Two records it as transforming into darkness in the Northern Dipper and governing right and wrong. Darkness is Ju Men's core label, and in classical Chinese the word means not yet clear, not yet settled, not evil.

Its meanings cover a cluster of words: inquiry, questioning, analysis, talk and expression. Ju Men's strength is not accepting surface explanations and being willing to follow things to the bottom; its cost is the same, because a probing way of speaking easily gives offence, and saying something too precisely can be harder to take back than saying it wrongly.

The *Complete Book* judges Ju Men harshly, listing unfavourable verdicts for it palace by palace, in the Siblings, Partnership and Parents Palaces among others. This book does not copy those verdicts. Its principles state that a palace's name is not an event, and forbid inferring a broken relationship from a single star; the old texts' heavy words serve here only as a hint of direction, not a conclusion.

Master Xiyi's phrase, handling right and wrong, is the more accurate reading: Ju Men is the star that deals with what is unclear. It is easily drawn into disputes, and is often the one who makes them clear.

When reading Ju Men, pay special attention to where Tai Yang is: sunlight dispels the dark, and old and modern readings agree on this point.

The *Complete Book*'s palace-by-palace verdicts on Ju Men are severe: in the Siblings Palace it speaks of kin estranged like stars that never meet, in the Parents Palace of being abandoned. This book does not use such language. Its principles state that a palace name is not an event, and forbid inferring broken relationships or what happens to family from a chart; those rules don't loosen just because the old texts speak with certainty.

What we keep is Ju Men's quality of expression, and the structural question of whether Tai Yang can shine on it.

star.天相.label: Tian Xiang
star.天相.summary: Tian Xiang belongs to Water and is the fifth star of the Southern Dipper. The *Complete Book* calls it the lodge that confers rank, transforming into the seal, a literary star of career. The seal means credentials and authorisation: Tian Xiang's position is support and execution, standing for systems, procedure and propriety. Master Xiyi says it gives a person ample food and clothing, and stresses that its position rises when it meets Wen Chang, Wen Qu, Zuo Fu and You Bi. Tian Xiang is rarely judged good or bad on its own; how it shows depends almost entirely on the two palaces that flank it. This is one of the few cases in Zi Wei Dou Shu where structure matters more than the star's own nature. What flanks it matters more than Tian Xiang itself, which is rare among the fourteen major stars. It belongs to Water, transforms into the seal, and the old texts class it as a literary star of career.
star.天相.full:
Tian Xiang belongs to Water. Book One of the *Complete Book* calls it the fifth star of the Southern Dipper, the lodge that confers rank, a star of blessing and goodness, transforming into the seal, a literary star of career in the position of assisting the emperor; the attribute table in Book Two records it as transforming into the seal in the Southern Dipper and ruling over career. The seal and assisting the emperor point to the same thing: Tian Xiang's role is authorising and carrying out, not deciding.

Its meanings cover a cluster of words: rules, coordination, propriety, reliability. Tian Xiang tends to get things done properly and keep every side satisfied; it is not good at conflict, nor at deciding for itself when there is no basis to go on.

Tian Xiang has one distinctive feature in how it is read: it is especially influenced by the palaces flanking it. What the old texts call the seal flanked by punishment and the seal flanked by wealth and shelter both say the same thing: the seal itself is neutral, and what matters is who is using it. This makes Tian Xiang the major star that most needs its structure read, and can least be judged by its own nature.

So whenever this book reads Tian Xiang, it explains the palaces on either side and its four directions, and states this dependence plainly. Taking Tian Xiang out on its own to judge it good or bad is the most common misreading of this star.

The two old patterns of the seal flanked by punishment and the seal flanked by wealth and shelter refer to what sits in the palaces on either side of Tian Xiang. The schools describe them fairly consistently, but the exact conditions still differ, so this book holds them back for review in its rules: the structure is recorded first, and the meaning waits for the sources to be completed.

It should also be said that transforming into the seal does not mean a job title or power. It describes a way of acting on authorisation, unrelated to any real-world rank.

star.天梁.label: Tian Liang
star.天梁.summary: Tian Liang belongs to Earth and is the second star of the Southern Dipper. The *Complete Book* says it governs longevity and transforms into shelter, blessing and long life; Book Two records it as transforming into shelter, a star of longevity. Shelter means covering and protecting: its meanings revolve around care, principle and taking on burdens for others. The *Complete Book* describes Tian Liang people as open and upright, and says it can turn violence into peace. Note that the other side of protecting is carrying: Tian Liang is often the one people come to. This book never reads governs longevity as a prediction about lifespan; its principles explicitly forbid that. When it falls in the Parents or Health Palace, the old verdicts are heavy, and this book reads them only as a structure of carrying for others.
star.天梁.full:
Tian Liang belongs to Earth. Book One of the *Complete Book* calls it the second star of the Southern Dipper, governing longevity and transforming into shelter, blessing and long life, ruler of parents, and says it turns violence into peace; the attribute table in Book Two records it as transforming into shelter in the Southern Dipper, a star of longevity. Shelter is Tian Liang's core label.

Its meanings cover a cluster of words: protection, principle, fairness, looking after others. Tian Liang tends to step forward, to take other people's difficulties on itself, and to handle things by a standard of its own. When the *Complete Book* calls it open and upright, it means exactly this unflinching stance.

The cost of protecting is carrying. Tian Liang's usual situation is not having trouble of its own, but having other people's trouble find its way to it; old and modern readings agree closely on this. And because it is used to standing on the giving side, Tian Liang often finds it hard to ask for help.

On governing longevity: this is the old writers' extension of the sheltering star, and this book never reads it as a judgement about how long anyone lives. Its principles explicitly forbid inferring lifespan, and that rule doesn't loosen even when the signals on a chart point the same way. Here Tian Liang is read only as a structure of protecting and carrying, never as years.

The *Complete Book* says Tian Liang rules over parents, and lists many heavy verdicts for it in the Parents and Health Palaces. This book never uses such verdicts to describe a reader's family or health: its principles set firm limits on language about health, and forbid inferring ill health or what happens to family. Tian Liang is read here as one thing only: a person used to standing on the giving side, and what that habit brings.

star.七殺.label: Qi Sha
star.七殺.summary: Qi Sha belongs to Fire and Metal and is the sixth star of the Southern Dipper. The *Complete Book* calls it the great general of the Dipper, and also the solitary star of success and failure. Book Two records it as a star of descent that gains authority when it meets the Emperor; those few words are the key to reading Qi Sha, because it needs guidance before its force becomes authority. Its meanings revolve around decisiveness, independence, and not avoiding conflict. The *Complete Book* judges Qi Sha harshly, calling it a malign star of the chart, but the same passage states that meeting Zi Wei turns it into authority: the condition is written out, not a final verdict. It always appears in the trines of Po Jun and Tan Lang, so Qi Sha is never an isolated star. It belongs to Fire and Metal, and its placement and the stars sharing its palace shape how it shows a great deal.
star.七殺.full:
Qi Sha belongs to Fire and Metal. Book One of the *Complete Book* calls it the sixth star of the Southern Dipper, the great general of the Dipper, the solitary star of success and failure, holding the Dipper's handle and governing law and discipline; the attribute table in Book Two records it as a star of descent in the Southern Dipper that gains authority when it meets the Emperor. Great general and solitary star side by side already say both its sides.

Its meanings cover a cluster of words: decisiveness, independence, bearing pressure, breaking new ground. Qi Sha has strong drive and is used to carrying things alone; it doesn't wait well and isn't keen on explaining. The solitary star describes the distance this tendency creates, not loneliness as a life sentence.

The *Complete Book* uses quite heavy words for Qi Sha, calling it a malign star of the chart, truly not a good star. This book doesn't pass such old language on to readers as it stands. The original goes straight on to state the condition, that meeting Zi Wei turns it into authority, which shows the old writers themselves saw it as a force needing guidance, not a fixed bad outcome.

In reading, Qi Sha forms a fixed trine with Po Jun and Tan Lang, and the three always see one another. So talking about Qi Sha almost always means talking about the whole group; reading one alone gives a skewed picture.

This book's principle with Qi Sha is to read it as drive and cost, never as calamity.

The old texts' heavy words about Qi Sha need a little background to be read accurately. When Zi Wei Dou Shu took shape, astrology's job leaned towards seeking good and avoiding harm, so the language naturally ran heavy; reading the same structure today, the emphasis should fall on what kind of action it describes, not on what end it foretells.

So this book neither writes Qi Sha as perilous nor, going the other way, as the mark of a strong person; both would be drawing conclusions for the reader instead of describing what is on the chart.

star.破軍.label: Po Jun
star.破軍.summary: Po Jun belongs to Water and is the seventh star of the Northern Dipper. The *Complete Book* calls it the spirit that governs spouse, children and servants, a star of expenditure in the chart, transforming into expenditure. Expenditure isn't loss but spending and renewal: its meanings revolve around breaking the old to build the new, restlessness with how things are, and willingness to tear down and start again. The *Complete Book* records it as strong in the Zi and Wu positions, and position makes a big difference to it. Po Jun forms a fixed trine with Qi Sha and Tan Lang, and the three always see one another, so reading Po Jun always means reading the whole group, never one star alone. Looking at one alone is sure to skew the reading. Transforming into expenditure means spending and renewal, not loss, a distinction that is clear in the classical language. It belongs to Water and is strong in the Zi and Wu positions.
star.破軍.full:
Po Jun belongs to Water. Book One of the *Complete Book* calls it the seventh star of the Northern Dipper, the spirit that governs spouse, children and servants, a killing force in heaven and a star of expenditure in the chart, hence transforming into expenditure; the attribute table in Book Two records it as transforming into expenditure in the Northern Dipper and governing spouse, children and servants. Both tie it to the closest relationships in a chart.

Its meanings cover a cluster of words: renewal, pioneering, breaking up old situations, putting in cost. In classical Chinese the word for expenditure means spending, not loss: Po Jun is willing to pay a price to get a new situation, which is both its strength and its risk. Stability is usually not Po Jun's goal.

The *Complete Book* records Po Jun as strong in the Zi and Wu positions, and the difference position makes is marked. When strong, its renewal has a direction; when weak, the same energy shows as back-and-forth and wear. That is a difference in strength and expression, not a verdict of good or bad.

Po Jun always forms a trine with Qi Sha and Tan Lang: if any one of them is in the Life Palace, the other two are bound up in its four directions. So when this book talks about Po Jun, it explains that structure at the same time; the three stars describe three faces of one quality: pushing forward, desire, and renewal.

It should be said plainly: Po Jun in the Partnership or Children Palace does not mean those relationships will break. The book's principles explicitly forbid that kind of inference.

The *Complete Book* says Po Jun governs spouse, children and servants; this is about which palaces it oversees, not a forecast of events. The book's principles state that a palace's name is not an event, and a triggered Partnership Palace does not mean a marriage will change. This book reads only Po Jun's tendency to renew and the cost it pays, never an outcome for a relationship.

Also, the name Qi Sha–Po Jun–Tan Lang is used quite differently across the schools, so this book holds it back for review in its rules until the sources are complete.

palace.命宮.label: Life Palace
palace.命宮.summary: The Life Palace is the starting point of the whole chart, placed by birth month and birth hour: count the first month from the Yin position, forwards to the birth month, then from there count the Zi hour backwards to the birth hour. In its essay on reading the stars, the *Complete Book* makes it the first step: first look at the Life Palace, at its fortunes, strength, transformations and the interplay of elements. The Life Palace describes the keynote of how a person handles things and their tendencies, not ability or achievement. Note that a Life Palace without a major star is not unusual; then it is read through the opposite palace, and this book always says so rather than skipping over it. The Life Palace faces the Travel Palace, and the two always come as a pair: one speaks of how you see yourself, the other of how the world outside meets you.
palace.命宮.full:
The Life Palace is set by birth month and birth hour together. Book Two of the *Complete Book* records the method: count the first month from the Yin position forwards to the birth month, then from the birth month count the Zi hour backwards to the birth hour, and place the Life Palace there. Once the Life Palace is set, the other eleven palaces follow in reverse order, and the chart's coordinates are fixed.

The essay on reading the stars sets out the order of reading clearly, and the first step is the Life Palace. The range of meaning this book allows is: keynote, way of handling things, what you ask of yourself. The Life Palace speaks of how a person tends to begin things and how they see themselves, not of what they can achieve.

A Life Palace without a major star is quite common. The *Complete Book* deals with it specifically: if the Life Palace has no major star, but the Wealth and Career Palaces have favourable stars shining on it, wealth and honour can still be complete. This book reads such a palace through the major stars of the opposite palace, and says so in the body of the book, in the form this palace holds no major star, so it is read through such-and-such in the opposite palace. An empty palace is itself information, and stating it plainly is more trustworthy than covering it up.

Finally: the Life Palace is not the whole life. It is one of twelve facets, and simply happens to be the one the count starts from. Reading the Life Palace as the whole of a person is the most common misreading in Zi Wei Dou Shu.

One more point of measure: however fine the stars in the Life Palace, they only give a tendency. Right after grading charts as high, middle and low, the *Complete Book*'s essay goes straight on to how the three directions meet and how strong the stars are; the old writers themselves never judged by the Life Palace alone. So when this book writes the Life Palace chapter, it always covers the four directions too, and says which parts come from the structure and which are only tendencies.

palace.兄弟.label: Siblings Palace
palace.兄弟.summary: The Siblings Palace comes right after the Life Palace in the order of the twelve palaces. The attribute table in Book Two of the *Complete Book* makes Tian Ji its ruler. The range of meaning this book allows is relationships with equals and working together: siblings, peers, people who stand beside you for a long time. The old texts mostly discuss how many siblings there are and whether they get on; this book doesn't use that, because a number is a question of fact that can't be inferred from a chart. Note that this book's principles state that a palace's name is not an event: malefic stars in the Siblings Palace don't mean trouble for your siblings, nor that the relationship must change. The palace isn't limited to blood relations; peers and long-term partners can be read here too.
palace.兄弟.full:
The Siblings Palace is found by counting one place backwards from the Life Palace, and Book Two of the *Complete Book* lists the order as first the Life Palace, second the Siblings Palace. The attribute table in the same book makes Tian Ji its ruler; Tian Ji transforms into goodness and governs turning things around, and that pairing already shows the nature of this palace: it speaks of how you deal with equals.

The range of meaning this book allows is: relationships with equals, cooperation, standing side by side, looking out for each other. It isn't limited to blood siblings; peers, long-term partners and colleagues can all be read here. This book's principles place the entry point for the theme of cooperation and community in the Friends and Siblings Palaces, which is exactly this.

Most of the *Complete Book*'s verdicts for this palace are about numbers and harmony, such as a certain star giving three or four siblings. This book never uses them. How many brothers and sisters someone has is a question of fact that can simply be asked, with no need to infer it from a chart; and the book's principles explicitly forbid inferring what happens to family from a chart.

In this palace, this book reads one thing only: what position a person tends to take among equals, whether leading, going along, or keeping a distance.

The palace also has a practical use today: together with the Friends Palace it belongs to the theme of cooperation and community, and helps in understanding a person's place in a small group. The book's principles require that theme to be cross-checked against the Career and Wealth Palaces and against interactions that have been verified; in other words, the Siblings Palace alone isn't enough to talk about cooperation, because how a person actually works and shares out resources matters too. In this chapter the book covers only the reader's own habits of working with others, and names the structures it relies on, so every sentence can be traced to its source.

palace.夫妻.label: Partnership Palace
palace.夫妻.summary: The Partnership Palace is the third of the twelve, called the palace of wife and concubines in the old texts. The attribute table in Book Two of the *Complete Book* records Po Jun as governing spouse, children and servants. The range of meaning this book allows is the patterns of close relationships: how you draw near, how you keep distance, what you care about. The old verdicts for this palace are heavy, and this book uses none of them: its principles explicitly forbid predicting that a marriage will break down, speaking for a partner, or counting marriages. Obstruction in the Partnership Palace does not mean a marriage will end; that is written in the book's principles. The palace describes the reader's own tendencies in relationships, not what a partner is like, and this book never assumes whether the reader has a partner.
palace.夫妻.full:
The Partnership Palace is third in order; Book Two of the *Complete Book* lists it as the palace of wife and concubines, which is the old name. The attribute table in the same book records Po Jun as governing spouse, children and servants: in the old writers' eyes these three palaces formed the closest circle of relationships.

The range of meaning this book allows is: the patterns of close relationships. How you draw near to someone, how you handle disagreement, what you care about most in a relationship. It describes the reader's own tendencies, not what a partner is like.

This is one of the palaces this book's principles govern most strictly. They state that Obstruction in the Partnership Palace does not mean a marriage will end, and forbid speaking for a partner or counting marriages; they place any certainty of a marriage breaking down behind a hard stop, which holds even when the birth chart, the decade and the year all point the same way. The *Complete Book* uses many heavy words for this palace, such as a certain star bringing harm to a spouse, and this book carries none of them over.

One more point: the Partnership Palace doesn't predict whether you have a partner, nor does it judge whether a relationship is good. The book's principles require that, when it's unclear whether a reader has a partner, the text either branches or leaves it out; this book would rather write one sentence less than assume anything about the reader's situation.

This book's approach is to write only tendencies that can be traced to the structure, and to keep the words on the reader's side. You tend to step back first in a relationship is a description whose source can be given; what your partner will do is not, and depends on your partner's own chart. That line holds throughout the relationship chapters.

It should also be said that this palace moves together with the Wellbeing and Life Palaces. How someone is in a relationship often has to do with how they settle themselves and how they see themselves. So this book covers the three together when writing about relationships, rather than treating the Partnership Palace as a standalone answer. What it writes is longer that way, but stands up better.

palace.子女.label: Children Palace
palace.子女.summary: The Children Palace is the fourth of the twelve. The attribute table in Book Two of the *Complete Book* records Po Jun as governing spouse, children and servants. The range of meaning this book allows is creation and continuity: your attitude to those younger than you, the work you pour yourself into, what you are willing to nurture. The old texts discuss how many children and whether there is harm to them; this book uses none of that, because the outcome of having children sits behind a hard stop in its principles, which holds even when all three layers point the same way. Here the palace is read only for the tendency to create, not for family members. Work, students and juniors all fall within this range, and the old texts' link between the Children Palace and creativity has its own basis.
palace.子女.full:
The Children Palace is fourth in order, and like the Partnership and Friends Palaces it is governed by Po Jun. The verdicts in Book Two of the *Complete Book* begin by saying that to read for children you first look at the stars in this palace to see how many sons there will be, and the whole passage revolves around the number of children and harm to them.

This book does not go down that road at all. The outcome of having children is one of the inferences this book's principles forbid, alongside lifespan, ill health and mishaps, behind a hard stop; the rule is clear that it holds even when the birth chart, the decade and the year all point the same way. It doesn't loosen because a chart's signals are strong, nor make an exception because a reader asks.

The range of meaning this book allows here is: creation, continuity, nurturing, investing yourself. The Children Palace describes what a person is willing to put their energy into, how they treat people younger or less experienced than themselves, and how they feel about leaving something behind. Work, students and juniors can all be read within this range.

This isn't evasion. The old texts' link between the Children Palace and creativity has its own basis; this book simply says clearly what can be said and sets aside, explicitly, what can't be inferred, rather than leaving it vague.

Also: the Children Palace is governed by Po Jun together with the Partnership and Friends Palaces, and the three form the closest circle of relationships. That means they often have to be read together: how a person treats those who come after them usually comes from the same ground as how they treat a partner and their peers. When this book writes these three chapters, they refer to each other rather than standing alone, and the book marks which structures they share, so readers can see that a palace appearing again is the same structure playing a role under a different theme.

palace.財帛.label: Wealth Palace
palace.財帛.summary: The Wealth Palace is the fifth of the twelve. The attribute table in Book Two of the *Complete Book* makes Wu Qu its ruler. The range of meaning this book allows is how you handle resources: how you earn, how you spend, how you judge what's worth it. Note that this book's principles state that income, assets and cash flow must not be confused, and no amount can be inferred from a chart. The Wealth Palace never answers how much money someone has; it answers what their relationship with money is. Any advice to buy, sell or borrow is explicitly forbidden by the book's principles. In financial decisions, real financial figures always take priority over the chart, as the principles put it.
palace.財帛.full:
The Wealth Palace is fifth in order. The attribute table in Book Two of the *Complete Book* makes Wu Qu its ruler, while Tian Fu and Tai Yin also rule over wealth and property. The essay on reading the stars lists it with the Travel and Career Palaces as the three directions: third, look at the stars of the Travel, Wealth and Career Palaces for clashes and harm. That arrangement already shows that the Wealth Palace can't be read alone.

The range of meaning this book allows is: how you handle resources. How a person earns, how they spend, what they're willing to pay for and what they can't bear to part with. It describes a habit, not a number.

This book's principles set a special requirement for this palace: income, assets and cash flow must not be confused. They are entirely different things, and talking about them together produces conclusions that simply don't hold. When writing the Wealth Palace chapter, this book handles them separately, and says plainly that no amount can be seen on a chart.

The line that most needs holding is this: on financial themes, a rating can only indicate a direction of meaning, never be enough reason to buy, sell or borrow. This book contains no specific investment advice, and never uses a chart to support or oppose a financial decision. In financial decisions, real financial figures take priority over the chart; those are the principles' own words.

The Wealth Palace forms the three directions with the Career and Travel Palaces, and the old writers had good reason to list them together: where money comes from, how you earn it and in what surroundings are three faces of one thing. So this book always covers all three when writing the Wealth Palace chapter, rather than reading one palace alone.

To repeat the measure once more: the Wealth Palace answers what a person's relationship with money is, not how much they have. The first can be seen on a chart; the second can't. Writing the second would be what the book's principles call false precision: buying credibility with a specific number that has no source.

palace.疾厄.label: Health Palace
palace.疾厄.summary: The Health Palace is the sixth of the twelve. The *Complete Book* reads it by looking first at the Life Palace and then at this palace, first checking whether the Life Palace's stars are weak and joined or faced by Qing Yang, Tuo Luo, Huo Xing, Ling Xing, Di Kong, Di Jie or Obstruction. This book treats this palace most conservatively of all: its principles set firm limits on language about health, and forbid inferring ill health or conditions of the body's organs. Here the Health Palace is read only as the direction of life's load and drain, with no description of any bodily condition and no risk grading of any kind. In this palace the book writes only where the drain comes from and how a person habitually handles long-term pressure, both of which can be traced to the structure of the chart.
palace.疾厄.full:
The Health Palace is sixth in order. Book Two of the *Complete Book* opens this palace with its method: first look at whether the Life Palace's stars are weak and joined or faced by Qing Yang, Tuo Luo, Huo Xing, Ling Xing, Di Kong, Di Jie or Obstruction, then judge the stars of the Health Palace by their nature and strength. It goes on to list bodily symptoms star by star.

This book uses none of that passage. Its principles place ill health and conditions of the body's organs behind a hard stop, alongside lifespan and mishaps, and go further in requiring that health themes never show any personal grading that resembles a clinical risk. This is the line this book will least of all let loosen.

So what is left to read in the Health Palace? The principles give the answer: the Health and Wellbeing Palaces together belong to the theme of life's load, noted as for reflection only, never as a clinical risk rating. So this book reads one thing only: where a person's drain comes from, and how they habitually handle long-term pressure.

This isn't vagueness. In this period you tend to carry things through to the end is a description that can be traced to the structure of a chart; take care of your stomach this year is not; it is a prediction dressed up as concern. This book keeps to that distinction throughout.

This palace is also where the book is most easily misunderstood as avoiding things. In fact the principles don't ask it to say less, but to say the right thing: describing long-term patterns of drain clearly is far more useful to a reader than an unfounded hint about the body. The first can be used to rearrange your life; the second only creates anxiety.

When writing this chapter, the book marks its sources of evidence with particular care, and ends each part by saying which parts come from the structure and which the reader should check against real life. On health, real medical information always takes priority over the chart, as the principles put it.

palace.遷移.label: Travel Palace
palace.遷移.summary: The Travel Palace is the seventh of the twelve, directly opposite the Life Palace. The *Complete Book*'s essay on reading the stars lists it among the three directions that must be read: third, look at the stars of the Travel, Wealth and Career Palaces for clashes and harm. The range of meaning this book allows is the outside environment and the circumstances you meet: how things are when you're away from home, how you deal with strangers, what conditions your surroundings give you. It pairs with the Life Palace: the Life Palace is how you see yourself, the Travel Palace how the world outside meets you. When the Life Palace has no major star, this is the palace it borrows from. The range isn't limited to moving: changing surroundings, facing unfamiliar situations and leaving familiar ground all count. When the Life Palace borrows from this palace, this book says so plainly.
palace.遷移.full:
The Travel Palace is seventh in order, and on the chart it always sits directly opposite the Life Palace. The *Complete Book*'s essay on reading the stars lists the Travel, Wealth and Career Palaces as the three directions that must be read, forming a core structure with the Life Palace.

The range of meaning this book allows is: the outside environment, the circumstances you meet, your relationship with unfamiliar settings. The Travel Palace describes how things are for a person once they leave familiar ground: going out, changing surroundings, meeting people they don't know, and whether conditions there are generous or tight.

The pairing of the Travel and Life Palaces deserves a word. The Life Palace speaks of an inner keynote, the Travel Palace of outside conditions; the two always come as a pair and always pull on each other. This is also why a Life Palace without a major star is read through the opposite palace: what it borrows are the Travel Palace's major stars. In that case this book says so plainly, because an empty palace is itself information.

There are two misreadings to avoid. One is reading the Travel Palace directly as moving house or emigrating: a palace's name is not an event, as the book's principles state clearly. The other is reading it as good or bad luck: the Travel Palace describes how generous or tight your surroundings are, and that means different things to different people.

A structural note: the Travel Palace belongs to the four directions together with the Life, Wealth and Career Palaces, and the book's principles require it to be cross-checked. This book uses it in both the Life Palace and Career Palace chapters, so readers will see the same palace in different chapters; that isn't repetition, but the same structure playing a role under different themes.

One more common way of writing to avoid: telling people with a strong Travel Palace that they should head out, and those with a constrained one that they should stay put. That is making decisions for the reader, which the book's principles explicitly forbid. This book describes only how generous or tight conditions are; whether to go or stay is the reader's own judgement.

palace.僕役.label: Friends Palace
palace.僕役.summary: The Friends Palace is the eighth of the twelve, called the palace of servants in the old texts and commonly the palace of friends today. The attribute table in Book Two of the *Complete Book* records Po Jun as governing spouse, children and servants. The range of meaning this book allows is networks and working relationships: colleagues, people who report to you, your circle. This book's principles state explicitly that it must not point out people who will do you harm; here the palace describes only the reader's own position and habits in a group, and never comments on any particular person. In Chinese this book keeps the traditional name, and notes both the old and modern names in the entry: the name stays, the reading follows modern working relationships between equals. It describes the reader's own place in a group.
palace.僕役.full:
The Friends Palace is eighth in order; Book Two of the *Complete Book* lists it as the palace of servants. That old name reflects the social structure of its time, and today it is commonly called the palace of friends. In Chinese, this book keeps the traditional name, like most Zi Wei Dou Shu books, so readers can compare; but it reads the palace in terms of modern working relationships, not as master and servant.

The range of meaning this book allows is: networks, cooperation, your position in a group. It describes how a person gets on with colleagues, people who report to them and people who share their interests, whether they tend to lead, go along, or go their own way.

The book's principles set one explicit prohibition for this palace: it must not point out people who will do you harm. This matters, because the old verdicts for this palace often lean that way, and readers are most tempted to match them to people they know. Once a book starts hinting that a certain kind of person can't be trusted, it stops being a book and becomes a way of setting people against each other.

So this book describes things only from the reader's side: what you tend to do in a group, what you expect, where you tend to spend your energy. What any person around you is like depends on that person, and isn't on this chart.

Together with the Siblings Palace, this palace belongs to the theme of cooperation and community, and the book's principles require both to be cross-checked with the Career and Wealth Palaces. Reading one palace alone for relationships gives a skewed conclusion. When writing this chapter, the book states the structures it relies on, so readers know where each sentence comes from.

It should also be said that the old name carries the clear mark of its era, and the old verdicts for this palace often assume a master–servant relationship. This book keeps the structure and drops that assumption: modern working relationships are level, and reading them as hierarchy is neither accurate nor useful.

In this chapter the book writes only about the reader's own position in a group and where their energy goes.

palace.官祿.label: Career Palace
palace.官祿.summary: The Career Palace is the ninth of the twelve. The attribute table in Book Two of the *Complete Book* makes Zi Wei its ruler, with Tai Yang, Lian Zhen and Tian Xiang each also having a part. The range of meaning this book allows is your way of working and how results show: how you do things, in what kind of structure you work well, what kind of results you value. This book's principles require this palace to separate ability from environment by structure, never mixing the two. The Career Palace doesn't predict job titles, industries or promotions. It describes a way of working, not an occupation; education, opportunity and real-world conditions are not on the chart at all. With the Life, Wealth and Travel Palaces it forms the four directions, the group that best explains how a person works.
palace.官祿.full:
The Career Palace is ninth in order and the most densely labelled palace in the *Complete Book*: the attribute table in Book Two records Zi Wei, Tai Yang, Lian Zhen and Tian Xiang all as rulers of career, or as rulers of career when placed there. This reflects how much the old writers valued this palace: in the era of the imperial examinations, career was almost the same thing as a person's place in society.

The range of meaning this book allows is: way of working, how results show, the kind of structure you work well in. It describes how a person does things, not what occupation they have.

The book's principles set one specific requirement here: separate ability from environment by structure. Whether someone's work goes well may be because they're good at it, or because their surroundings give them a lot; on a chart these are carried by different structures, and mixing them gives misleading conclusions. When writing the Career Palace chapter, this book covers the two separately.

What to avoid is reading the Career Palace as a job title or an industry. A palace's name is not an event, and actual career choices involve education, opportunity, relationships and real conditions, none of which are on the chart. This book never advises readers to change jobs or resign; that is something its principles explicitly forbid.

The Career, Life, Wealth and Travel Palaces make up the four directions, the combination that best explains how a person works. This book always covers all of them in the Career Palace chapter: the Life Palace is method, the Wealth Palace cost, the Travel Palace environment, and the Career Palace where results show. Reading one palace alone for a career gives a conclusion without conditions.

One more point: the old writers valued the Career Palace because in the examination era social position was almost everything about a person. That isn't so today. This book puts it back in its place as one facet: it explains how a person works, not what a person is worth.

palace.田宅.label: Property Palace
palace.田宅.summary: The Property Palace is the tenth of the twelve. The attribute table in Book Two of the *Complete Book* has Tian Fu and Tai Yin both ruling over wealth and property. The range of meaning this book allows is settling and belonging: where you live, how you arrange your home, your attitude to holding things for the long term. This book's principles state explicitly that it must not be equated with buying property; a triggered Property Palace does not mean buying a home. Here the palace is about how a person settles themselves, not whether they'll own property. The range isn't limited to real estate: a rented home, a city you've stayed in for years, even a studio can all be read here. The old texts also used this palace for the atmosphere at home; this book writes only about the reader's own attitude, never about family members.
palace.田宅.full:
The Property Palace is tenth in order. The attribute table in Book Two of the *Complete Book* records Tian Fu as ruling over wealth and property, and Tai Yin as ruling over wealth and property too: two stars of preserving and gathering in govern this palace together, and the direction is clear.

The range of meaning this book allows is: settling, belonging, holding things for the long term. It describes how a person arranges their base in life: putting down roots or staying mobile, treating home as a place to rest or as something to build. It isn't limited to real estate: a rented home, a city you've stayed in for years, even a studio can all be read here.

The book's principles set a very specific prohibition: it must not be equated directly with buying property. This has real consequences, because buying a home is a major financial decision, and the principles explicitly forbid using a chart to support decisions of that kind. A line like the Property Palace is active this year being read as a sign to buy is an entirely possible misreading, and this book won't offer the opening.

The Property Palace is also often used for the atmosphere at home. This book handles that carefully: describing the reader's own attitude to home is fine; commenting on family members is not.

The Property, Wealth and Wellbeing Palaces pull on each other structurally: resources, settling and contentment are three facets of one set of questions. When writing the Property Palace chapter, this book covers them together, and says plainly which parts are tendencies and which depend on real conditions.

There's also a way of writing to avoid: telling people with a constrained Property Palace not to buy, and people with a strong one that they should buy. That is making financial decisions for the reader, which the principles explicitly forbid. This book describes only a person's attitude to settling and long-term holding; actual decisions involve real conditions that aren't on the chart.

When writing this chapter, the book marks the structures it relies on.

palace.福德.label: Wellbeing Palace
palace.福德.summary: The Wellbeing Palace is the eleventh of the twelve. The *Complete Book*'s essay on reading the stars makes it the fourth step, noting that it faces the Wealth Palace: fourth, look at Authority, Abundance, Di Jie and Di Kong in the Wellbeing Palace and their strength, because the Wellbeing Palace faces the Wealth Palace. The range of meaning this book allows is state of mind and enjoyment: what settles you, what drains you. With the Health Palace it belongs to the theme of life's load, which this book's principles mark as for reflection only, never clinical assessment, so the book never describes emotional conditions in this palace. The Wellbeing Palace faces the Wealth Palace: one speaks of inner contentment, the other of outer resources, two sides of the same coin.
palace.福德.full:
The Wellbeing Palace is eleventh in order, and the attribute table in Book Two of the *Complete Book* makes Tian Tong its ruler. The essay on reading the stars makes it the fourth step of reading a chart, and points out that it faces the Wealth Palace. That contrast is interesting: one speaks of inner contentment, the other of outer resources, two sides of the same coin.

The range of meaning this book allows is: state of mind, enjoyment, how you settle yourself. The Wellbeing Palace describes what a person relies on to feel settled: quiet, company and bustle, getting things done, or having someone there. In return, it also points to where the drain comes from.

This book's principles list the Wellbeing and Health Palaces together under the theme of life's load, noted as for reflection only, never as a clinical risk rating. The book holds to this closely: the Wellbeing Palace is never used to describe emotional conditions, and nothing resembling a psychological assessment appears. A person's mental health belongs to professionals, not to a chart.

In this palace, the book writes only what can be traced to the structure: in what state a person tends to feel things are right, and what kind of situation takes particular effort.

The Wellbeing Palace is also the main way in for judging whether a person is tired, but tired here means how mental energy is spent, not a health condition. The principles draw that distinction clearly, and so does this book: describing tendencies is fine, assessing someone's state is not. The difference is that the first can be traced to the structure, and the second needs professional judgement.

When writing the Wellbeing Palace chapter, the book puts the weight on what can be acted on: under what arrangements this person spends less of themselves. That's something a reader can take away; a judgement about emotional state is not.

palace.父母.label: Parents Palace
palace.父母.summary: The Parents Palace is the last of the twelve. The *Complete Book* treats Tai Yang as the father star and Tai Yin as the mother star, and lists many heavy verdicts for this palace. This book uses none of them: its principles explicitly forbid inferring misfortune for a reader's parents from the reader's chart. The range of meaning this book allows is a single one: the reader's own relationship with elders, authority, paperwork and rules. How family members fare depends on their own charts, not this one. The old texts also used this palace for documents and rules; this book keeps that use, because it truly fits the structure. This palace faces the Health Palace, and the book uses that pairing only to understand the reader, never to infer anything about family.
palace.父母.full:
The Parents Palace is twelfth in order. Book Two of the *Complete Book* opens this palace with its method: in reading for parents, take Tai Yang as the father and Tai Yin as the mother. It then lists verdicts of harm one by one, in very heavy language.

This book uses none of it. Its principles are explicit: no inferring a third party's ill health, lifespan or character, and no inferring from a reader's chart that their parents, partner or children must meet misfortune. This sits behind a hard stop, which doesn't loosen when signals on a chart point the same way, nor make an exception because a reader asks.

The range of meaning this book allows here is a single one: how the reader gets on with elders, authority and rules. Whether they tend to comply or push back, whether they're used to being looked after or looking after others, whether they go around systems or by the book: these are all descriptions of the reader, and can be traced to the structure of the chart.

The old texts also treated the Parents Palace as the palace of documents, and this book keeps that use: its relationship with rules, paperwork and formal procedure genuinely fits this palace's structure.

Reading the Parents Palace as what will happen to one's parents would be writing someone else's life into the reader's book. This book doesn't do that.

One structural detail in passing: the Parents Palace sits directly opposite the Health Palace on the chart. The old writers developed many verdicts from this, which this book likewise doesn't use, for the same reasons. Here the pairing is used only to understand the reader: how you face elders and how you face your own drain are often two sides of the same pattern. In this chapter the book writes only about how the reader deals with rules and elders.

sihua.祿.label: Abundance
sihua.祿.summary: Abundance is the first of the four transformations. The *Complete Book* records Master Xiyi as saying that Abundance is the spirit of blessing: placed in the Life, Body or Career Palace and meeting Recognition and Authority, it is sure to bring high office. In this book's reading, Abundance means resources opening up and things getting under way; it describes flow and ease, not an amount. Note that the original also says that even malign stars, Qing Yang, Tuo Luo, Huo Xing and Obstruction clashing with it do no harm, a very confident tone; this book doesn't carry that confidence over. A single Abundance is not enough for any conclusion, as the book's principles state. Which palace it falls in, and which layer sets it off, says more than whether it is Abundance or Obstruction.
sihua.祿.full:
Abundance is set off by the heavenly stem of the birth year. Book Two of the *Complete Book* lists it stem by stem in its verse on the four transforming stars: for the Jia stem, Lian Zhen turns to Abundance, Po Jun to Authority, Wu Qu to Recognition and Tai Yang to Obstruction, and so on for the rest. Book One records Master Xiyi as saying that Abundance is the spirit of blessing: placed in the Life, Body or Career Palace and meeting Recognition and Authority, it is sure to bring high office.

The range of meaning this book allows is: resources, going with the current, things getting under way. Abundance points to something having the conditions to move: the road clears, the people arrive, the money is found. It does not promise an outcome, and it does not refer to any amount.

The old texts speak of Abundance very optimistically, even saying that malign stars do it no harm. This book doesn't carry that confidence over. Its principles are clear: a single Abundance is not enough to judge that things will go smoothly, still less that money will come. Which palace it falls in, which layer sets it off, and whether other evidence points the same way: without all of these, no conclusion can be drawn.

The three layers of transformation must be read separately: the birth-year transformations are the long-term background, the decade's are the theme of ten years, and the year's are that year's trigger. The same star turning to Abundance in different layers speaks of things on different timescales, and they can't be stacked as three votes; the book's principles require them not to be double-counted.

One last point of measure: Abundance and wealth are not the same thing. Wu Qu rules over wealth; Abundance is resources opening up. The two can appear together or separately. Reading Abundance straight as being rich swaps a structural description for a promise about numbers, which is exactly what the book's principles call false precision. When this book talks about Abundance, it talks only about flow and conditions, never sums.

sihua.權.label: Authority
sihua.權.summary: Authority is set off by the heavenly stem of the birth year. The *Complete Book* records Master Xiyi as saying that the star of Authority is the spirit that holds the power to judge and decide: placed in the Life or Body Palace and meeting Recognition and Abundance, it brings command in war and office in peace. The meaning this book allows is driving forward, taking responsibility, having the say: it describes a force that steps in, able to decide and answerable for it.
